prologue.title: Now
prologue.subtitle: A machine shed, two hours of gravel from town

norway.title: Norway
norway.subtitle: A fjord in the west, about the year 870

knows_he_bled.description: Aud said the uncle left bleeding, and that somebody in the hall did it

hrapp_owes.description: You kept the smith alive in front of the hall

walter.name: Walter
walter.notes: Your uncle. The hall calls him Unkel, having taken the word for his name.

kol.name: Kol
kol.notes: A boy of about eleven, with a dog. He finds everything first and tells everyone.

thorgrim.name: Thorgrim Ketilsson
thorgrim.notes: The hersir. It is his hall, and his half pound of silver.

aud.name: Aud Ketilsdóttir
aud.notes: Thorgrim's sister. The keys are hers.

hrapp.name: Hrapp
hrapp.notes: The smith. He does your uncle's voice.

welder.label: A welder
welder.description: You join steel for a living and have the forearms to prove it. You have never done it without electricity.

nurse.label: A nurse
nurse.description: Eleven years on a surgical ward, most of them nights. You know what a wound ought to look like on the third day.

teacher.label: A history teacher
teacher.description: You have explained the fall of Rome to fifteen-year-olds every spring for nine years. Nobody has asked you to prove any of it until now.

engineer.label: An engineer
engineer.description: You can say why a bridge stands up and what it will cost. Other people have always done the building.

rider.label: Rode as a child
rider.description: Every Saturday until you were sixteen. Somebody else always caught the horse, and somebody else fed it.

charm.label: Easy to like
charm.description: People tell you things. You have never been sure what you do to cause it, and have learned not to ask.

martial.label: Martial arts
martial.description: A brown belt, earned twice a week in a hall that smelled of feet. Nobody there was trying to kill you.

fencer.label: Fenced
fencer.description: Three years of foil, with a mask, a referee and a rule about whose turn it was.

speaker.label: Used to a room
speaker.description: You can stand up in front of two hundred people and be heard at the back. What you said when you got there has varied.

hunter.label: Hunts
hunter.description: A week every autumn, with a rifle and a flask, and the truck forty yards behind you.

sailor.label: Sails
sailor.description: Summers on a lake, in a boat that belonged to somebody's father. You know where the wind is before you know you have looked.

farm.label: Raised on a farm
farm.description: Chores before school for sixteen years. Animals have never frightened you, and have never impressed you either.

tall.label: Tall
tall.description: You have found most door frames the same way.

slight.label: Slight
slight.description: People hand you things to hold.

broad.label: Broad
broad.description: Strangers ask you to help them move house.

blunt.label: Blunt
blunt.description: You say it, and afterwards you find out whether you should have.

quiet.label: Quiet
quiet.description: You are often taken to be agreeing.

cheerful.label: Cheerful
cheerful.description: It has been held against you.

first_night.label: The first night
first_night.description: This is as far as the prototype goes. The visit, the other two eras and the four years are still to be built.

n_hill.title: The hill
n_hill.text:
You are up to the shins in heather and the rain is coming in from the side.

The frame has not come with you, nor the shed. Behind you is a boulder about the size of a grain truck, with a streak of white quartz down the face of it, and you take a good look at that streak, since it is the only way home you know about.

Somebody has been at the quartz with a nail. Cut into it, at about the height of a short man's shoulder, are a letter and a row of marks.

::clue boulder_tally::

You count them twice. You had thought he had only done this the once.

Then you turn around, and it is some time before you do anything else.

The hill falls away below your boots in grey rock and rusty bracken, down to water that lies a long way under you, black-green and so still that it holds the mountains upside down. It runs inland between walls of rock that go up into the cloud and do not come out again. Across from you a waterfall hangs on the far wall, a white thread of it, too far off to hear.

There is no wire anywhere in the sky and no road cut into the other shore, and it is quieter than you knew a place could be. You would have liked somebody to be standing next to you, to say so to.
[break]
On a shelf of green by the water stands a building, longer than your uncle's shed and much lower, bowed along its length like the hull of a boat turned over. Grass is growing on the roof. Smoke leaks out along the ridge, having found no chimney, and lies down flat in the rain. Smaller roofs stand about it, and strips of field gone pale with stubble, and on the shingle below are two boats drawn up side by side. Even from this height you know the line of them, the long rise to the stem that somebody drew in one stroke.[if trait.sailor]

The wind is coming up the water from the sea, and the smoke agrees with you. Both boats have been hauled out with their sterns to it, by somebody who did not have to look either.[/if]

The only other one you have seen was in a museum, black and cracked, propped on steel behind glass. These two are the colour of dark honey and they are wet. Whoever built them is very likely down there under the grass roof, keeping dry, and could build you a third if you had anything to pay him with.

You try your phone. It has sixty-one per cent and nobody to call, and you put it away.

By now you are cold enough to notice. You get into the lee of the boulder and collect sticks, with some confidence, having lit fires before, in a pit, on a dry evening, with a firelighter. Wet heather held over the lighter gives off steam. The bark of a small bent birch does no more. You take out the note and consider it, and decide your uncle would want it kept. By the time the lighter is too hot to hold you have produced a smell.
[break]
"Hvat ertu?"

A boy is standing a few yards up the hill with a dog and a stick. He might be eleven. His wool is the colour of the hillside, which accounts for how near he has got, and the dog beside him has plainly reached a decision about you and is waiting for him to catch up.

The brass thing clicks twice behind your ear, like a relay closing.

"What are you?" he says again. This time it reaches you in English, half a beat after his mouth has finished. He has asked what, you notice, and not who.

[if manner == blunt]"Cold," you tell him.[elif manner == quiet]You hold up your hands, which have gone the colour of the boulder, and let him work it out.[elif manner == cheerful]"Cold, thanks," you tell him, as you might to somebody at a bus stop.[else]"Lighting a fire," you tell him, over the place where there is no fire.[/if]

[if manner == quiet]He frowns at you as people do at the hard of hearing.[else]Your throat does something to the words on their way out that you had no part in, and he frowns as people do at a heavy accent.[/if] Then he looks at your sticks, and at the lighter, which you are slow to cover.

He crouches down. Out of the pouch on his belt come a curl of steel, a flake of stone and a pinch of black felted stuff, and with his back to the wind and a knee on your sticks he has a flame going before you have the lighter back in your pocket. He feeds it with bark he has been carrying inside his shirt, where it keeps dry. His hands manage all this alone, because the rest of him is studying your jacket.
[break]
"Can I?" he says, and has hold of the zip before you answer. He runs it down and up and watches the teeth shut behind the tab, and does it again, eleven times in all. You keep count, there being nothing else for you to do at your own fire.

"Unkel had one of these," he says. "On his trousers."

"You know my uncle?"

"Everyone knows Unkel. He owes Thorgrim a ship."

After that he gets round to what you are carrying.

[if kit == bag]He has it open before you can decide whether to stop him.

[if occupation == welder]The helmet he puts on, and takes off again directly, having found that it makes the world dark. The gloves he approves of. Then he comes to the file. He tries its edge with his thumb and draws it once along the back of his fire-steel, where it lifts a bright curl and leaves a flat, and he looks at the flat for some time.

"You are a smith," he says. "Hrapp is our smith." He puts the file back with more care than he took it out. "Hrapp is going to hate you."[elif occupation == nurse]The scissors he approves of. The gloves he blows up, ties off and gives to the dog, which does not want one. Then he finds the stethoscope, and after some thought puts the wrong end in his mouth. You fit it to his ears and hold the other end against his chest. He listens to himself for a while, and afterwards to the dog, and you can see him deciding which of them is the better made.

"You are a healer," he says. "Gyda is our healer." He hands the thing back by its tubing, as he would a live eel. "Gyda is going to hate you."[elif occupation == teacher]It holds thirty-one essays on the causes of the First World War, which you had meant to mark at your uncle's kitchen table. He turns over a good many pages before he sees that the marks on them are all different, and that somebody made every one. The red pen he clicks until you take it from him. He draws a line with it across the back of his hand and holds the hand out to the rain to see whether it will stay.

"You make marks for remembering," he says. "Ulf remembers for us, and he needs no marks." He gives you back the essays, in no order. "Ulf is going to hate you."[else]The hard hat he puts on and keeps on. The calculator he shakes, in case there is something in it. Then he finds the tape, draws out an arm's length of it, and lets go. When it has finished coming back at him he does it again, and then he measures the dog, which is forty-one inches from nose to tail and holds still for it.

"You measure things," he says. "Orm builds our ships and he measures nothing. He looks." He winds the tape in by hand, slowly, to see where it goes. "Orm is going to hate you."[/if]

He appears to be looking forward to it. He says he is called Kol, and he carries the bag down the hill himself, shouting before the yard is in earshot that he has found something on the mountain and that it was he who found it.[elif kit == notebook]It is open on your knee, where you had been hunting for a page about fire. This is the page you have instead.

::clue notebook_people::

"You're Kol," you say.

The boy stops with his hand on the dog's neck. "Who gave you my name?"

You have no answer he would like, so you hold up the book. He looks at the marks on the page as he might at the tracks of an animal he had only been told about, and he does not come any nearer to them. Your uncle has gone round the last line a good many times, you notice, and not all with the same pen.

Kol goes down the hill well ahead of you and does not wait at the turns. When you reach the yard on your own, a good while after him, a number of people have found work to do near the door, and it is clear that the news has arrived and that it was about the names.[else]He looks into it and is not much struck. You tear a corner off the sugar and shake some into his palm, and he takes it for salt and licks it up out of manners.

He stands quite still. Then he cleans the palm thoroughly, looks into the sack to see how much more of it there is, and ties the neck himself, with a knot you would not like to have to undo.

"Do not give that to anybody on the way down," he says. "They will only want it."

He lets you know that he is called Kol and that you may walk behind him. In the yard he informs a woman carrying buckets, and after her the hens, that the stranger is his, that he found it, and that nobody is to touch the sack.[/if]

n_hall.title: Unkel's water
n_hall.text:
Your boots were made for a flat floor, and you go down most of the hill sitting.[if trait.rider]

There is a horse in the yard, about the size of a large pony and the colour of the hill. It looks you over as the ones at the riding school used to, and you can tell that it has come to the same view.[/if]

The door of the long building is cut for people who know where the lintel is.[if looks == tall] You find out where it is.[elif looks == broad] You go through it at an angle, as a sofa would.[elif looks == slight] You pass under it with room to spare, and it is the last thing you do all day as well as the people who live here.[/if]

Inside it is dark and far bigger than it looked from the hill. A fire burns in a trench down the middle of the floor, a truck-length of it, and its light climbs the posts and gives up before it reaches the roof. The posts are whole trees. Somebody has carved every one of them, from the floor to as high as you can see, with beasts that bite each other and are knotted so tight you could not get a nail in between. It is the best thing you have ever seen made by hand, and nobody in the room is looking at it. The place smells of smoke and wet dog, of meat and of a good many people, [if looks == forgettable]none of whom has turned round. You stand inside the door for long enough to learn the price of a ewe. In the end it is a small child who points.[else]some thirty of whom have turned to look at you. The talk stops one bench at a time, working up from the door to the far end, until the fire is the loudest thing in the room.[/if]
[break]
Near the hearth sits a man with his sleeve pushed up and a cut across the heel of his hand. An old woman has him by the wrist, and a girl is lifting a pot off the fire between two sticks.

"Eighteen," the girl is saying. "Nineteen. Twenty. That is four."

"That is three," says the man with the hand.

"It is four, Bjorn. I have my thumb on it."

"Then your thumb moved."

They count it again to settle the matter. Only when the girl has reached twenty does the old woman pour, and the man lets his breath out through his teeth, and she ties up the hand in a cloth out of the same pot.

"Unkel's water," Kol says, in the tone of a boy with a slow pupil. "You boil it for a hundred. Nobody is going to count a hundred for a pot, so we count twenty, five times." He lifts his chin at the man. "Bjorn put an axe in his own leg last winter and it should have come off. Unkel washed it in his water every day and shouted at anybody who touched it, and Bjorn still has the leg."

"Did he say why it works?"

"He said there are beasts in water, too small to see, and the boiling kills them." Kol considers you, to find out whether you are the kind of person who would believe that. "Nobody listened to that part. But the leg stayed on. So we boil it, and we leave out the beasts."
[break]
At the head of the fire, in the only seat with a back, a man of about fifty has watched your arrival without moving anything but his eyes. He is built along the same lines as the posts. He lifts one finger, and you go up the hall.

[if kit == bag]"Kol tells me he has found something useful," Thorgrim says. "The last one off that hill told me he was useful as well."[elif kit == notebook]"Kol tells me you had his name before he gave it," Thorgrim says. "Have you mine?" You have, and you say it, and the people on the bench nearest you discover that there is room further along.[else]You put the pepper and a card of needles on the board in front of him. He opens the tin and sneezes, and is pleased with it. "Unkel came with his hands empty and went away with them full," Thorgrim says. "You have it the other way about."[/if]

"You are his kin, though. You have his clothes, and you stand in my hall as he did, as if somebody were about to explain it to you." There is some laughing at this. "He ate at my fire from hay-time until the leaves turned, and he ate well. He kept Bjorn's leg on, and reminded us of it most evenings. I liked him. He said he could build me a ship that would sail into the wind. I asked how, and he drew it in the ashes, and it was a handsome drawing. I gave him half a pound of silver to buy iron. Six nights ago he went up that hill with it and has not come down."

"What do you want with a ship that sails into the wind?"

"There is a king working his way along this coast," Thorgrim says, "and he has the wind behind him. Tonight you are my guest. Tomorrow you are Unkel's kin, and you have what Unkel owes. We will talk about my ship when you have eaten."
[break]
[if hero.sex == male]You are given the end of the bench nearest the door, among the dogs, where a stranger sits until the hall has made up its mind.[else]You are given the end of the cross-bench at the far wall, where the women of the house sit, and where you are gone over a good deal more thoroughly than Thorgrim troubled to.[/if]

A girl brings you a basin of water and a cloth and holds them out. You look at the basin and then at the girl. It has been a long day, and you cannot honestly say whether the water is for drinking. You settle it by wiping your hands down your jeans, to show you mean well.

A woman has stopped behind the girl to watch this. She is about your age, in a dress of the dark red that a gate goes when it has rusted properly, with the sleeves shoved back from work she has not finished, and at her belt hangs a ring of keys, a dozen or more. People along the benches drew in their feet as she came. Her face, through the whole business with the basin, stays exactly where it was, and you suspect that took some doing.

"Hands in the water," she says. "After that the cloth, and after that you eat. Unkel had it by his second month."

A bowl arrives with something grey and hot in it, and barley in that. No spoon arrives. Along both benches people are taking spoons out of belts and sleeves, having brought their own, as people evidently do. She unhooks one of pale horn from beside the keys, worn thin along one edge, and holds it out, and keeps hold of her end when you take yours.

"I have had this longer than I had my husband," she says. "I want it back."

Kol informs you, at no great pains to be quiet, that this is Aud, Thorgrim's sister, and that the keys are hers and so is whatever they open.

n_choke.title: The smith's throat
n_choke.text:
Across the fire a man with burned forearms has been telling his end of the bench about Unkel, and doing the voice. He does it well. You know it for your uncle at once, through a brass ear and eleven hundred years, and you find that you have missed the sound of him. Halfway through a sentence about the ship he stops.

Nobody minds at first. He has a mouthful, and a man with a mouthful is allowed to stop. Then he gets to his feet, and puts a hand flat on the board, and the other to his throat, and makes no sound at all. The man next to him laughs and thumps him between the shoulders. The smith's face has gone the colour of a plum.

[if occupation == nurse]You have done this eleven times, twice on the same patient, and you are over the bench and round the fire before you have decided to be.[else]You once spent a wet afternoon in a church hall being shown this on a rubber torso by a man called Keith. You find, to your surprise, that it took.[/if]

You get behind him, put your arms round his middle, make a fist under his ribs with the other hand over it, and pull.
[break]
It is only now, with your arms round a stranger from behind in a hall full of his kin, that you see how it looks. Three men are on their feet. One of them has a knife out, the short one he was eating with, and is coming round the end of the bench with it. You pull again, and something leaves the smith at speed and lands in the fire, where it hisses.

He breathes in, with a noise like a door being forced. Then he calls you something the brass ear declines to translate.

Nobody in the hall is talking. The man with the knife has stopped, though he has not put it away.

"What," says Thorgrim, "did you do to my smith?"

choices.text: Tell him it is a hold your people use for a bone in the throat.
Tell him the man was choking and now he is not, and sit down.

n_hold.title: A hold
n_hold.text:
"It is a hold," you say. "Where I come from it is taught for a bone in the throat. The fist goes here, under the ribs, and you pull up and in."

Thorgrim nods slowly. A hold is a thing a hall understands. They wrestle here all winter, having little else to do, and the man with the knife puts it away and asks to be shown where the fist goes.

You show it on Kol, who has volunteered by standing closest. Before the bowls are empty there are three pairs of boys by the door doing it to one another, and one of them has been sick. The old woman who poured the water comes down the hall to ask whether there is a word that is said with it. You tell her there is not. She is disappointed in you, and you gather from Kol that there will be a word by tomorrow whether you supply one or not.
[break]
Aud sits down on the bench beside you, which makes the bench go quiet.

"'Where I come from it is taught,'" she says. "That was well put. Unkel would have told us why it works, and Hrapp would have died of listening."

"It is taught, where I come from."

"I do not doubt it." She takes back her spoon, looks it over, and hangs it by the keys. "Hrapp will not thank you. He hates to owe, and he liked Unkel less than anybody here did. I would stay out of the forge for a day or two."

n_silent.title: Your barley
n_silent.text:
"He was choking," you say. "Now he isn't."

You step back over the bench, sit down and pick up your bowl, which is still warm.

For a little while nothing happens. After that the hall does your explaining for you, at some length, and you eat through it. By the time you reach the bottom of the barley you have been a wrestler from the east, and you have been one of Unkel's people, who are known to have healing in their hands. The old woman who poured the water holds that you squeezed a thing out of Hrapp that had been in him since midwinter, and that he is better without it. Nobody asks you which. Thorgrim has you moved four places up the bench, into the warm, and somebody you have not met fills your cup.
[break]
Aud comes for her spoon when you have finished with it.

"You let them tell it," she says. "Unkel never once managed that. He would have been on his feet by now, drawing in the ashes."

"There wasn't much to tell."

"No." She turns your hand over, looks at the palm as if it might say more than you had, and gives it back. "I will want to hear it, all the same. It need not be tonight."

n_explain.title: Two pipes
n_explain.text:
"There are two pipes in the throat," you say. "One is for air and the other is for food. The meat went down the one for air. There was still air in his chest, under the meat, so I squeezed the chest, and the air pushed it out."

Bjorn feels his own neck with his good hand. The old woman who poured the water asks, quite reasonably, why in that case a man cannot breathe and swallow together all day long. You tell her there is a flap that closes.

"A door," says someone further down. "In the throat."

"A small one."

You hear it, then, as they are hearing it. Thorgrim looks at you for a time without unkindness.

"Unkel talked like this," he says. "The beasts in the water."
[break]
Hrapp, who owes you his life, has moved a place further down the bench from you. Several people have found something to look at in their bowls. Aud takes you by the sleeve, walks you the length of the hall to the door post, and stands with her back to the room.

"Was it true? About the pipes."

"Yes."

"I thought it might be. Unkel's were mostly true as well." She keeps her voice under the noise, which is starting up again behind her. "They will have a true thing out of your hands any day of the year. Out of your mouth it is only talk. The last one here who talked like that went up the hill six nights ago with his hand wrapped in his shirt."

"Whose knife was it?"

"Eat your barley," Aud says. "And I will have my spoon back when you have."

e_first_night.title: The first night
e_first_night.text:
The fire is banked for the night, and the hall goes to sleep around you all at once, as a barn does. Rain is falling on the grass over your head. It is a roof you would very much like to tell your mother about, and you have been asked not to.

[if kit == bag]Your bag is under your head, and you have a hand through the strap.[elif kit == notebook]The notebook is inside your jacket, where nobody can ask to see it.[else]Kol has the sack, and is asleep on top of it.[/if] [if shown.craft >= 1]By the door, two boys are still practising the hold on each other in the dark.[elif shown.open >= 1]Further down the bench somebody is still explaining you to somebody else, and getting it wrong.[else]Nobody has lain down within an arm's length of you.[/if]

Tomorrow you are Unkel's kin.

p_shed.title: The shed
p_shed.text:
Your uncle Walter does not trust telephones, so the news comes by post, on one page, in block capitals pressed hard enough to read from the back.

::clue letter::

He has ended every letter that way since you were nine, including the Christmas cards, which he addresses to her. You are the only person he writes to, and you have never been sure whether to take that as a compliment. He did not say which Saturday. You let that carry you past the first one, and it is the second when you go.

It is two hours of gravel to his place. The yard light is on at noon and his truck is in the yard with the flat you mentioned in April, when he said he was aware of it. The shed door is rolled open a foot for the cat.

Inside, the heater is running for nobody. There is a cup of coffee on the bench with a skin on it, and the radio is on low, where a man is reading out the price of canola.
[break]
Bolted to the slab in the middle of the floor is a door frame, with no door in it and no wall around it. It is seven feet of two-inch square tube, and cables as thick as your wrist run from it to a rack of equipment you cannot name, apart from one item, which is the arc welder that went missing from your mother's garage four years ago. He helped you look for it.

[if occupation == welder]You look at the welds first, because you always do. You gave him a summer of lessons once, and none of it stuck. He has ground every joint flat and painted over it, and nobody does that to a weld they are proud of. Whatever this frame does, those are what is holding it together.[elif occupation == nurse]You look at the bench first, because eleven years have taught you to find the mess before you look at the patient. There is a roll of gauze with its wrapper torn open by teeth, a bottle of the brown antiseptic nobody has stocked since you trained, and a tea towel that will not be used for tea again. Whatever he cut, he dressed it one-handed and in a hurry, and about as well as he does most things.[elif occupation == teacher]You look at the shelf first, because you read people's shelves. There is the Old Norse grammar you lent him two Christmases ago and wrote off, with its spine broken at the verbs. Next to it are a road atlas of Italy and a paperback history of Japan with a bus ticket a third of the way in. He has never been known to finish a book, and you would have said he had never been known to start three.[else]You look at the supply first, because somebody ought to. The cables run back to the panel by the door, where he has pulled the breaker for the grain dryer and fitted something of his own made out of copper bar. There is a scorch on the wall above it in the shape of a hand. Nothing in this building is rated for whatever goes through that frame, and the building has plainly told him so.[/if]

Under a wrench on the bench is half a sheet of paper.

::clue note::

There is a thumbprint beside the W, in something brown. You would like it to be coffee, and coffee does not dry that colour.
[break]
Beside the note is a foam-lined case cut for two of something. One place is empty. In the other is a brass object about the size of a hearing aid, with a hook to sit behind the ear. He has put a strip of masking tape on the lid.

::clue ear_label::

There is a label just like it on the dash of his truck, and you have ridden in the truck.

Through the frame you can see the back wall of the shed, the pegboard and the co-op calendar, all where they belong. The air inside it is a little darker than the air outside it, though, as it is in any doorway, and a draught is coming through that smells of woodsmoke and low tide. The nearest tide is three days' drive from here.

The cat is on a blanket against the far wall, which is as far from the frame as a cat can get without going out in the rain. It has the look of an animal that settled there some days ago.

There is more tape on the frame itself, at eye height.

::clue frame_label::

So you are going, it seems, and the question is what the hand is for. Your work bag is in the truck, since he asked for it. His notebook is on the bench beside the note, a black one gone fat with use, with a rubber band round it. And over the kettle is a shelf he has labelled TRADE, which holds a bag of sugar, a tin of pepper and three cards of steel needles from the fabric shop in town. You had taken that for groceries and a hobby.

choices.text: Fetch your work bag from the truck.
choices.text_after:
The bag is on the passenger seat, under a coat, where it spends its weekends.

You hook the brass thing behind your ear and find it warm, as if it had lately been behind somebody else's. The note goes into your jacket, since a person should have something to show the police. Your phone and your lighter are in your pockets already, where they live.

You step through the frame as you would over a garden hose, without looking down, with your one hand's worth.

The notebook is heavier than it looks, and it smells of his truck.

You hook the brass thing behind your ear and find it warm, as if it had lately been behind somebody else's. The note goes into your jacket, since a person should have something to show the police. Your phone and your lighter are in your pockets already, where they live.

You step through the frame as you would over a garden hose, without looking down, with your one hand's worth.

choices.text: Empty the TRADE shelf into a feed sack.
choices.text_after:
The sugar, the pepper and the needles go into a feed sack from the pile by the door. They leave a good deal of sack.

You hook the brass thing behind your ear and find it warm, as if it had lately been behind somebody else's. The note goes into your jacket, since a person should have something to show the police. Your phone and your lighter are in your pockets already, where they live.

You step through the frame as you would over a garden hose, without looking down, with your one hand's worth.

door.label: New game
door.summary: Your uncle wrote to say he finally got it to work.

creation.title: Who went through the door
creation.lede: Your uncle wrote to you, and not to anybody else. He will have had a reason.

sex.owed: Say whether you are a man or a woman.

courts.prompt: And if you were to lose your head over somebody
courts.note: Two people in each era can be courted. Nobody has to be.

groups.prompt: What you do for a living
groups.owed: Say what you do for a living.

groups.prompt: Two things about you that have never once been useful
groups.full: Two only. Put one back first.

groups.note: This and the next change how you are written about more than what happens to you.

creation.name_long: That name is too long for the envelope.

place: Nobody has decided what you are.
You have a place by the door, and a use.
You have been moved up the bench, into the warm.
talk: Nobody is talking about you yet.
They are talking about you, kindly enough.
They are explaining you to each other.
People move along the bench when you sit down.
They are saying what they said about your uncle.

kits.sack: A feed sack of sugar, pepper and needles

letter.title: The letter
lines: BRING WHAT YOU USE AT WORK.

note.title: The note on the bench
lines: If I am not, DO NOT FOLLOW.

notebook_people.title: A page of his notebook
lines: KOL. Boy, about 11. Dog. Finds everything first, tells everyone.
AUD. His sister. Do not bother lying to her.
